title: Birth, schooling, Gulf Coast summer, saxophone, and forming the Owls
summary: White gives his birth (1901, New Orleans), schools and Tulane, then tells of the Gulf Coast hotel summer where he took up saxophone, the weekend jam sessions and the start of the band.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: We'd better go back to the beginning and start at the beginning of your life. The embarrassing question. When is your birth date?
When is it? When is it?
It's on August the 30th. You mean when I was born?
1901. 1901. It's a long while ago. 59 years ago.
And were you born in the city?
Yeah, born right here in New Orleans.

I was born originally on First Street. And we moved from there to Valmont. We moved many times, various locations. Of course, Pine Street was the... I was actually, as a boy, I can recall my life on Calhoun, 1467 Calhoun Street, which was quite a neighborhood for young boys. We had, I guess, about 25 youngsters, all about the same age, within a radius of two city blocks there. We went to LaSalle Grammar School. I'd rather LaSalle... Yeah, the Grammar School. And then, of course, when high school came in, most of us were lost. Well, our friendship was split up, because I went to Newman Manual Training as part of my high school, and then went up east to Williston in East Hampton, Massachusetts, to complete my high school studies. Finally wound up with two years at Tulane University here in New Orleans. In the College of Commerce and Business Administration, I believe it was right at the beginning of the Business Administration. I know my uncle was one of the... Well, anyway, they called on certain business houses to sort of underwrite the College of Commerce and Business Administration when it first started, and he was one of those that was in that original group that underwrote that college. Yeah, old Dean Aldrich was a dean at that time. I remember going before him many times, because I wasn't the most brilliant student in the College of Commerce and Business Administration. We did a little playing while we were at Tulane. We had a little orchestra up there. It was more fun than anything else. Had no idea of playing professionally at all. That, our idea of playing professionally... Rather, we never had an idea of playing professionally, but we used to get together. Funny thing, there was a band here, not a band, but a string outfit called the Six and Seven Eights, if you recall, which Dr. Sushong was just on This Is Your Life, as you recall. And some of our boys who were with us were in that. For instance, Red Mackey was one of them that was with the Six and Seven Eights. Eblen Rowe was one that was with the Six and Seven Eights. Monk Smith, who is now dead, was with the Six and Seven Eights. Well, at the same time, we had a little string outfit. Originally, I played violin. And we were playing on the... We had a summer vacation on the Gulf Coast. We played three days a week at the Miramar Hotel and passed Christiane, and three days a week at the Belmar Hotel in Mississippi City, I think that's what it was, between Gulfport and Biloxi. A fellow by the name of McLaughrey, as I understand, owned it at that time. And there was a chap here in New Orleans who got this engagement by the name of Guy Lyman. He's passed away now. He couldn't play any instruments, but he loved to play drums. But he didn't even own a set of drums. He had nothing but just an ordinary crate with a bunch of cans and things hooked on it. Believe it or not, there were... Let's see, there was Eugene DeBall, or Jinx as we call him, Jinx DeBall. There was a fellow by the name of Fred Ogden. There was Eblen Rowe, Guy Lyman, and me. And we went over this summer to play at these two hotels. And that was our first experience in the professional end of music. It was really a holiday for us, we enjoyed it immensely. And that's where I started playing saxophone. We used to go down to Biloxi and listen to the band at the Hotel Biloxi, and they had a saxophone player in there who I thought was very good. So one weekend I came back to New Orleans and went to one of the huck shops here and bought a saxophone. Went over to Whirlines and bought a new mouthpiece for it. I didn't know who'd been blowing it. And took it back over the Gulf Coast with me and started blowing that thing. And boy, I never got so much razzing in all my life. Got old socks and everything else put in it that quieted me down. Finally, I learned how to play the thing. Well, our summer over there was a rather nice vacation. And we came back. And then we started playing some of the group. Eblen Rowe, Monk Smith, came out of the 6 and 7 8s. And Rene Jalpe, and I, I don't recall some of the others, but we used to play on weekends out at West End at what was then known as the Agnes Boathouse. It was in the pen where they keep these yachts. The name of Daddy McKnight, as I recall, owned that. And we used to go out there every Saturday night and just play for our own benefit. We'd have a good time out there. And from that, Red Mackey and his brother, Dick Mackey, who played the cornet. Red played the, was playing the bass with the 6 and 7 8s, but he also played piano. There was Red Mackey and Dick Mackey, his brother, Monk Smith, who played the saxophone at that time. Rene Jalpe, who played banjo. And I got together to form a little, a little band. And we played for a subscription dance, as I recall it, down at the old Courtshade Club, down in the French Quarter. We didn't make any money, but we had a lot of fun. And from there, we played one or two engagements, started to play a few engagements, at the old rowing club, which used to be out at the end of the, out at the, Biosync John here. They had regular dances out there, which we played for. And then, I recall one incident, and I don't recall, I'm not sure of the name of the girl, I'm, I know her very well, but I'm not too positive about it, so I don't want to mention her name. But anyway, she was the debutante of the year. And she had a debutante party. And she asked us if we'd mind playing for the debutante party. And we told them, no, we wouldn't mind. So we went to play for this debutante party. And she had engaged Guy Lyman's orchestra, who was here on the Orphium Circuit at that time. He was playing at the Orphium Circuit. Well, he came out to the country club, New Orleans Country Club. And we were there, and we put our instruments down, and went, sat down with the rest of the guests, because we're all personal friends of them. And he wanted to know, how we rated, uh, eating with the rest of the guests. Well, we weren't out there playing, for, professionally, we were out there enjoying ourselves. It was quite a party. But from then on, we began to get engagements of spot jobbing around at various places, and, and began to actually sell the band. Then, I never will forget, one day, we went down to the Roosevelt Hotel, Earl Crone, who was drummer at the time, with us, and I went down there. I don't know, I can't, I really don't know why we went down, but we went down to see about playing in the, what was then, the Venetian Room. And we talked to the manager, whose name was Weber, and he said, well, fine, come on, we'll start right away. You fellas got a nice following, so we went to work in the, in the Venetian Room. And we'd play all winter long in the Venetian Room. When that was over, we'd go in the summer, out to the West End Roof Garden, and we played, if, I hope I'm correcting this, about four seasons, alternating between the Venetian Room, and the, and the West End Roof Garden. We had a marvelous, time along, because it was all a big happy event with us. We were just a bunch of school kids, having a, a big time. Hi guys. I'll never forget one night, we were on the West End Roof Garden, and, this chap, by the name of, now what is his name, he owned this big, home out here in City Park. Um, I can't think of his name, I was a big oil man here. Anyway, he called up the West End Roof Garden, wanted to know if they had a big crowd out there, and he said, no, we don't have too many, and I said, we'll close it up. I want the band out at my home, in City Park, he was throwing a party. So they closed up the West End Roof Garden that night, and we went out and played all night long, till six o'clock in the morning, and then left there, and went from there out to the, because another one of the guests, who was,
